items.abstract_text: The rapid proliferation of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has radically disrupted higher education assessment paradigms (Chung, 2024). Institutional responses to maintaining assessment integrity have primarily focused on defensive mechanisms, such as mitigating risks surrounding written assessments, refining text-matching software, and enforcing restrictive academic integrity policies (Lodge, 2024). However, this reactive posture often overlooks the transformative potential of GenAI as a student’s and lecturer’s long-term coach in authentic assessment design (Atif, 2024). This research-in-progress pivots away from deficit-based AI detection, proposing instead the integration of VirtualSpeech GenAI avatars to converse with students during a recorded viva, generating verifiable, real-time student output. By replacing static written tasks with dynamic oral assessments, this relatively new form of creative expression maintains authentic student contributions to improve AI literacy, strengthen authorship verification, eliminate academic outsourcing, and simultaneously cultivate sophisticated negotiation skills (Perkins, 2026). This study represents an exemplary innovation of practice by reframing AI not as an academic threat, but as a dual-mode learning and assessment avatar. Rather than engaging with AI purely for text generation, students interact with GenAI avatars (such as VirtualSpeech) simulating realistic corporate stakeholders. This work is strongly anchored in the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework, which guides the deliberate alignment of GenAI technology, modern pedagogy, and discipline-specific knowledge (Mishra & Koehler, 2006). This framework assists educators in leveraging immersive technology to redefine pedagogical delivery, facilitating AI literacy and negotiation skills. This research addresses a critical gap in current Technology Enhanced Learning (TEL) literature by investigating the following central question: How are students’ AI literacy and negotiation skills developed when conversing with GenAI avatars as part of a viva presentation? Adopting a design-based research methodology, this project emphasizes the iterative refinement of an educational intervention within an authentic setting (Hoadley & Campos, 2022; Scott et al., 2020). The study is currently in its first implementation cycle within a major tertiary institution, featuring a sample size of 150 second-year Project Management students. Participants are required to defend a project proposal during a live, assessable viva presentation conducted with a customized VirtualSpeech avatar trained to act as a client. This oral format diminishes the appeal of cognitive offloading because students must defend their reasoning under unseen, real-time questioning (Sotiriadou et al., 2020; Tan, 2026). Data collection relies on a mixed-methods approach, utilizing pre- and post-intervention surveys alongside qualitative analysis of student reflections. Preliminary quantitative results indicate a statistically significant increase in both self-reported IT literacy, validating the avatar’s efficacy as a formative and summative tool. This research significantly advances TEL research and practice by providing a protocol for proactive AI integration. While piloted within a project management curriculum, broad applicability across tertiary contexts exists (Cela-Ranilla, 2025). Any discipline requiring high-stakes communication, critical thinking, and stakeholder management—such as business, law, or education—can adapt this viva model. Ultimately, this work demonstrates how universities can safeguard academic integrity not by restricting technology, but leveraging it to create robust, future-focused verbal assessments, requiring students to perform and defend understanding live.

items.abstract_text: The rapid emergence of generative artificial intelligence (AI) presents significant challenges in higher education, often leading to student dependency and educator “AI fatigue.” Despite policy calls for assessment reform, practical, evidence-based approaches to developing critical AI literacy remain limited. This paper addresses this gap by presenting a practice-based curriculum case study and reflective inquiry investigating the structural redesign of a multidisciplinary Information and Communications Technology (ICT) unit. Moving away from surveillance and AI detection, the curriculum was redesigned to decompose high-stakes assessments into a scaffolded, low-stakes formative feedback sequence. Employing a Reflective Teaching Practice (RTP) methodology grounded in Schön’s reflective practitioner framework, the inquiry evaluates this curriculum redesign through the educator’s professional reflective diary and theoretical student persona modelling. Theoretical learning archetypes were constructed to evaluate how the scaffolded structures support diverse student AI literacy profiles. Educator reflective logs highlighted strategies for managing AI dependency and inflated expectations around AI, suggesting that scaffolded AI literacy and personally relevant assessments helped mitigate cognitive offloading. Ultimately, this inquiry suggests that navigating the AI landscape requires a return to foundational, compassionate pedagogical principles, prioritising continuous feedback and structured self-reflection to support positioning AI as a meaningful learning opportunity rather than a disruptive academic burden.

items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) occupies two positions in talent development simultaneously: the principal driver of the reskilling imperative, obsoleting skills faster than organizations can replace them, and increasingly the instrument through which reskilling is delivered, via adaptive platforms, generated content, and automated coaching. Reskilling scholarship assumes training technology is causally independent of the skill shift it responds to, an assumption prior industrial transitions permitted but AI's shared mechanism no longer does. This conceptual paper argues that AI's dual position generates five failure modes conventional reskilling models cannot detect: velocity without capability, a deskilling loop in which the instrument reproduces the condition it was deployed to remedy, personalization that fragments collective capability, stratified access that widens the divide reskilling was meant to close, and erosion of the entry-level roles through which experiential learning occurs. Drawing on integrative reviews of AI and workers' skills, Industry 4.0 reskilling blueprints, and AI governance scholarship, the paper applies the HUMAN framework (Human Oversight, Upskilling for AI Literacy, Meaningful Augmentation, Accountability and Audit, Networked Learning) to each failure mode, and extends its upskilling principle into a three-tier AI literacy architecture, operational fluency, evaluative literacy, and complementary capability, that depreciates at rates inverse to the investment it typically attracts. The paper translates this into five testable propositions and offers implementation guidance differentiated by organizational context.

items.abstract_text: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into teacher education has brought both opportunities and challenges. While AI tools are increasingly accessible to pre-service teachers, excessive dependence on AI may inadvertently undermine their critical thinking disposition—a key competency in professional development. Based on social cognitive theory, this study investigates the influence of AI dependence on pre-service teachers’ critical thinking disposition, with a particular focus on the mediating role of AI self-efficacy and the moderating role of perceived stress. A three-phase longitudinal design was employed. The study tracked 461 pre-service teachers from Jiangxi Province, China. Data were analyzed using structural equation modeling (SEM) to examine the hypothesized relationships, including the mediation effect of AI self-efficacy and the first-stage moderating effect of perceived stress. Results showed that AI dependence significantly and negatively predicted pre-service teachers’ critical thinking disposition. AI self-efficacy partially mediated this negative association. Furthermore, perceived stress significantly moderated the first stage of the mediation process, such that the negative association between AI dependence and AI self-efficacy was stronger among pre-service teachers with higher levels of perceived stress. The conditional indirect effect was stronger at higher levels of perceived stress, and the index of moderated mediation was significant. The second-stage moderation was not significant. These findings highlight the potential risks associated with excessive AI dependence in teacher education: over-reliance on AI may undermine pre-service teachers’ critical thinking disposition partly through reduced AI self-efficacy. Moreover, perceived stress amplifies the negative indirect effect by moderating the first stage of the mediation process. This study extends social cognitive theory to the context of AI use and provides practical implications for promoting balanced AI engagement and critical thinking development in teacher training programs.

items.abstract_text: The growing integration of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) into intellectual activities is transforming how individuals acquire information, solve problems, generate ideas, and make decisions. Although these systems can substantially expand access to cognitive resources, their effectiveness depends not only on technological capabilities but also on users’ ability to regulate their own thinking during human–AI interaction. A central challenge is determining which cognitive activities should be performed independently, which can be delegated to artificial intelligence, and under what conditions AI-generated outputs require independent verification. This conceptual paper examines metacognitive management of human–AI interaction as a dynamic process involving cognitive self-awareness, strategic delegation, ongoing monitoring, critical evaluation, and reflective adjustment. Drawing on classical theories of metacognition, cognitive offloading, trust calibration, and contemporary research on human–AI collaboration, the paper proposes the Metacognitive Delegation and Verification Cycle (MDVC), a six-stage framework for regulating AI involvement in cognitive activities. The framework distinguishes between task execution and cognitive responsibility, arguing that effective delegation does not necessarily entail the abandonment of independent reasoning. Instead, appropriately regulated interaction allows individuals to distribute cognitive effort while preserving their capacity to evaluate evidence, recognize uncertainty, revise decisions, and maintain intellectual autonomy. The paper further introduces a task-sensitive delegation typology, a risk-adjusted verification strategy, and practical metacognitive questions designed to support users before, during, and after AI-assisted activities. Potential applications are examined in education, scientific research, professional reasoning, and everyday decision-making. Finally, testable propositions and methodological directions are presented for future empirical investigation. The central argument is that the development of human–AI collaboration should be evaluated not only through improvements in immediate task performance but also through the quality of cognitive regulation, independent understanding, and the preservation of human judgment

items.abstract_text: The rapid integration of large language models (LLMs) into higher education has intensified debate over how AI-assisted learning may be associated with students’ cognitive development. Although prior studies have examined the benefits and risks of AI use, less attention has been paid to the distinction between frequent AI usage as a learning behavior and large language model dependence (LLMD) as a habitual reliance on LLMs for cognitive and academic tasks. This study therefore distinguishes frequent AI usage as a learning behavior from LLMD as a habitual reliance on LLMs when completing cognitive and academic tasks. Drawing on the Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) model and Conservation of Resources theory, this study examined how AI usage is associated with university students’ critical thinking through LLMD, metacognitive awareness, and AI literacy. Survey data were collected from 878 Chinese university students and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling. The results showed that AI usage was positively associated with LLMD, which represented the strongest direct association in the model, while LLMD was negatively associated with metacognitive awareness, AI literacy, and critical thinking. The mediation analysis further indicated a significant negative total indirect association between AI usage and critical thinking through LLMD and lower levels of metacognitive awareness and AI literacy. These findings contribute to the literature by clarifying the distinction between AI usage and LLMD and by identifying metacognitive awareness and AI literacy as cognitive resources associated with critical thinking in AI-assisted learning contexts. Practically, the study suggests that universities should move beyond simple restriction-oriented responses and pay greater attention to the quality of students’ AI engagement, including metacognitive monitoring, AI literacy, and awareness of dependence-related patterns.

items.abstract_text: The rapid emergence of autonomous artificial intelligence agents, predictive supply chain orchestration, and real-time cross-border regulatory analytics is fundamentally transforming how multinational enterprises (MNEs) govern global value chains (GVCs) and enter foreign markets. Yet International Business (IB) higher education remains largely tethered to twentieth-century pedagogical paradigms—relying on static international trade models, retrospective written case studies, and essentialist cultural heuristics that fail to prepare graduates for algorithmically mediated global commerce. Moving beyond surface-level classroom adoption of generative chatbots, this study develops a comprehensive theoretical and operational framework for re-engineering International Business education through the lenses of Global Value Chain Governance Theory, Activity Theory, and Metacognitive Scaffolding. We argue that the defining competency for next-generation IB professionals is Algorithmic Value-Chain Orchestration—the ability to align predictive and generative AI systems with cross-jurisdictional institutional realities, geopolitical risks, and culturally grounded human judgment. To operationalize this capability, the paper introduces a Three-Horizon Curricular Transformation Architecture alongside a Synthetic Global Commerce Laboratory that immerses students in dynamic multi-tier supply chain disruptions, automated customs and rules-of-origin auditing, and cross-cultural digital platform governance. Drawing upon longitudinal pedagogical implementations across undergraduate and postgraduate IB cohorts, we demonstrate significant gains in students' systemic risk reasoning, critical verification of algorithmic outputs, and cross-border strategic adaptability. Finally, the study examines structural challenges—including cognitive atrophy, Western-centric training data biases, and cross-border data compliance—and establishes an institutional governance charter for sustainable business school transformation.

items.abstract_text: BACKGROUND: Reliance on AI-supported health recommendations is consequential, but a single behavioral source-selection decision is not equivalent to multidimensional psychological trust. Biosignals may contain predictive information before a choice, although small-sample multimodal models require leakage-free evaluation and cautious interpretation. PURPOSE: This study evaluated whether facial-expression probabilities and galvanic skin response (GSR) features predict a task-specific binary choice of an AI-labeled rather than doctor-labeled recommendation in a simulated ADHD assessment. The outcome is treated as a behavioral indicator of reliance rather than a direct measure of psychological trust. Method: This cross-sectional laboratory analysis included a cohort of 60 participants (40 AI-labeled and 20 doctor-labeled choices). Eight facial-expression probabilities and two GSR phasic features were evaluated in prespecified Early (6-3 s) and Proximal (3-0 s) windows. Ten repeats of participant-level stratified five-fold cross-validation were used. Scaling and SMOTETomek resampling occurred only within training folds, and the logistic stacking meta-learner was trained on strictly cross-fitted base-model probabilities. Model-specific 95% confidence intervals and paired AUC differences were estimated with 10,000 stratified participant bootstrap samples; five paired tests were Holm-adjusted. RESULTS: Early-window ROC-AUCs were 0.643 (95% CI 0.490-0.786) for Face, 0.430 (0.287-0.578) for GSR, and 0.526 (0.375-0.679) for stacking. Proximal-window ROC-AUCs were 0.550 (0.399-0.699), 0.381 (0.240-0.530), and 0.376 (0.229-0.529), respectively. Stacking did not outperform either modality. Early stacking was worse than Early Face (ΔAUC = -0.116, 95% CI -0.183 to -0.056; Holm-adjusted p = 0.002); the other adjusted paired comparisons were not significant. CONCLUSION: Multimodal stacking did not improve prediction in this small exploratory sample. These results do not establish either a general advantage or a lack of value of multimodal fusion. They do not support deployment or direct trust detection. Larger studies with verified synchronization, repeated decisions, independent trust measures, and external validation are required.

items.abstract_text: Higher education is confronting an academic-integrity challenge unlike any in its history. Students can now outsource homework, take-home assignments, and online examinations to large language models (LLMs) that complete them in seconds. Existing research on evaluating LLM performance on academic assessments has focused largely on standardized examinations, or on questions from college-level courses drawn from a single discipline. Far less is known about how LLMs perform on college-level assessment questions spanning multiple disciplines, that instructors have purposely designed to be AI-resistant, and about which features of such questions, if any, meaningfully constrain LLM performance. We address this gap by collecting 75 questions from authentic college coursework assessments, spanning 17 disciplines, which were contributed by 37 faculty members from ten U.S. universities and one U.K. university. Of these, 61 questions were intentionally designed by faculty members to be 'LLM-proof', while the remaining 14 questions were sourced from online courses. We then (i) evaluate three state-of-the-art LLMs' ability to correctly answer these questions with and without supplementary course materials; (ii) identify five strategies, through thematic analysis, that faculty used to make their questions harder for LLMs to solve; and (iii) test whether these strategies impact LLMs' ability to answer the questions accurately. Our experimental results show that the best-performing model scored approximately 83% without supplementary course materials and 85% with them, and we observed noteworthy differences across models, answer formats, and instructor tweaking strategies. We discuss implications for assessment design, academic-integrity policy, and the broader ethics of deploying LLMs in educational settings.

Instead, it helps manage cognitive load during demanding modules for learners who are good at self-regulated learning. items.abstract_text: This study examined the effects of Generative AI (GenAI)-assisted learning on the critical thinking skills of higher secondary school students. A quasi-experimental pre-test and post-test design with a non-equivalent control group was used. The sample consisted of 59 Grade XII students of Garrison Academy Kharian Cantt (Army Public School and College), Punjab, Pakistan: 28 girls in the experimental group and 31 boys in the control group. For one month, the experimental group was taught with GenAI tools (Claude and DeepSeek) and the control group was taught with traditional methods. Critical thinking was measured before and after the teaching period with a 30-item Critical Thinking Questionnaire based on Facione's (1990) six skills: interpretation, analysis, evaluation, inference, explanation, and self-regulation. The data were analysed with paired-samples t-tests, independent-samples t-tests on gain scores, and analysis of covariance. The total critical thinking score of the experimental group rose from M = 72.71 (SD = 5.11) to M = 121.25 (SD = 7.79), t(27) = 29.02, p < .001, d = 7.37, and that of the control group rose from M = 68.68 (SD = 7.75) to M = 77.58 (SD = 8.03), t(30) = 8.15, p < .001, d = 1.13. The mean gain of the experimental group (48.54 points) was significantly larger than that of the control group (8.90 points), t(57) = 20.21, p < .001, d = 5.27, and the analysis of covariance, which adjusted for the pre-test score, gave the same result, F(1, 56) = 466.24, p < .001, partial η² = .893. All six skills improved more in the experimental group. For classroom practice, the result suggests that guided GenAI activities, in which students compare AI answers, check them against the textbook, and give their own reasons, are worth adding to regular teaching under the teacher's supervision. The effect sizes were unusually large, the experimental group also started higher than the control group (p = .023), and the pre-test reliability of the questionnaire was low (α = .29). The findings should be read with care because the groups were intact classes that also differed in gender. items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly entering adult and continuing education, where it can explain, summarise, draft and evaluate on the learner's behalf. The quality of work produced with AI assistance may therefore rise while the learner's own understanding, judgement and critical thinking remain unchanged or decline. This conceptual article examines how AI-assisted adult learning can preserve learner autonomy, independent judgement and critical thinking while still benefiting from generative tools. It builds on Natseva's distinction between functional cognitive offloading and higher-order cognitive outsourcing and integrates it with research on learner autonomy, self-regulated learning, metacognition, automation bias, critical-thinking instruction and the learning–performance distinction, drawing on a purposive, non-systematic literature selection that is reported transparently. The original contribution is the AI-Assisted Autonomy and Critical Thinking Assessment (AACTA) framework, which specifies six assessable dimensions: prior independent reasoning, purposeful AI engagement, appraisal of AI output, cross-source contrast, decision ownership, and unaided demonstration and transfer. Each dimension is operationalised as a scoring rubric with observable indicators at three levels, from displaced to autonomous, together with a procedure for training two assessors and checking their agreement. AACTA is compared with existing measures of learner autonomy, self-regulated learning and critical thinking. The framework is accompanied by a dual-outcome principle, which requires AI-assisted performance and unaided learning to be measured separately, and by a provisional assistance-gap index. Five testable hypotheses are formulated, and a three-arm randomised study with a preceding pilot and multi-context replication is proposed as future work. The framework has not been empirically validated, and no data were collected for this article.

items.abstract_text: Critical thinking has been a cornerstone of education. Some wonder what these technological advancements will do to people’s thinking and, more specifically, to critical thinking. In this chapter, we look at some of the potential affordances and limitations to critical thinking regarding artificial intelligence (AI) and how educators might respond. We address three aspects of critical thinking as outlined by research. First, critical thinking is the capacity to problem-solve. AI has the potential to help solve problems, although it might also erode one’s abilities, what some researchers call “cognitive offloading.” Second, critical thinking is a social process where people come together to think and challenge ideas. AI and newer technologies in general might bring people together; however, they might lead to what we are calling social offloading. Third, critical thinking is dependent on a diversity of ideas. Generative AI has the potential to synthesize a diversity of information and provide greater access; however, its models and algorithms may slowly limit this diversity. We situate these conceptions of critical thinking in concert with AI and provide pedagogical considerations for music educators to move toward a more process-based approach to critical thinking. This includes creating purposeful moments for students to work collaboratively—or to gather—and think critically, while also using AI tools.

items.abstract_text: This paper reports preliminary findings from a redesigned capstone assessment in a first-year Management unit at an Australian university involving over 300 students. items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has become increasingly embedded in university students’ learning practices, yet its implications for student well-being remain insufficiently explored. This literature review synthesizes existing evidence on the potential benefits and risks of generative AI use for university student well-being and examines the psychological mechanisms that may explain these relationships. The reviewed literature suggests that when generative AI is used as a learning-support tool, it may contribute to reduced academic stress, stronger learning confidence, greater learning efficiency, emotional support, and greater satisfaction with task completion. In contrast, when AI substitutes for rather than supports core cognitive processes, its use may be associated with over-reliance, diminished autonomous learning, academic-integrity concerns, AI-related employment anxiety, and technostress. Self-efficacy, cognitive offloading, academic stress, and autonomy emerge as important psychological mechanisms through which generative AI use may relate to student well-being. Overall, the relationship between generative AI use and student well-being does not appear to be uniformly beneficial or harmful but varies according to how, why, and to what extent students use AI. Future research should therefore move beyond whether students use generative AI and examine more precisely the patterns and conditions of use that support or undermine student well-being.

items.abstract_text: Generative AI poses a risk to students’ creative thinking when it is adopted without critical reflection (Elgammal, 2026). These tools are marketed as collaborators and tutors, offering constant and largely uncritical encouragement (Chow & Celis Bueno, 2025; Walsh 2025). This presentation holds the promise of AI partnership alongside evidence that these tools displace cognitive and creative effort (Gerlich, 2025; Temler 2026). This problem is widely recognised, but proposed responses remain inconsistent, vague or untested. Many calls to address the use of generative AI correctly identify the problem or alternatively show singular approaches and case studies. What is needed is a discipline-agnostic framework on building students’ awareness of their own creative processes in the context of these tools. The approach offered here to develop creativity with AI has two theoretical foundations: Margaret Boden’s theory of creativity and art, and the Kolb Experiential Learning Cycle (2011) as a pedagogical approach. Boden (2004 distinguishes combinational, exploratory and transformational creativity: the recombination of existing ideas, movement within a conceptual space, and alteration of that space’s defining dimensions. Novelty can be either new to the individual or new more generally under this view. Boden argues that novelty may come about in several ways, including combining existing ideas in new ways, exploring or changing existing ideas, or transforming dimensions of those ideas. The two frameworks do different work. Boden supplies the criteria students apply when judging whether their output is genuinely novel, surprising and valuable; Kolb supplies the cycle through which that judgement is made repeatedly and acted upon. Without Boden, reflection has no object; without Kolb, the criteria are applied once and forgotten. Students work through Kolb’s (2011) four stages in their learning: concrete experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualisation, and active experimentation. These each serve a cumulative purpose in developing the students’ collaborative process with generative AI. In the first phase, the student does their first draft of a creative process, using AI in any way they want to experiment with. Afterward, they reflect on that experience, considering questions about what skills they developed (or did not), whether the draft did what they wanted it to do, and how they felt about the AI tool use. Based on this reflection, they can then develop and express a personal set of beliefs on practical use of generative AI. Finally, they can try out a new approach based on these conclusions – which then become the next concrete experience. It is an ongoing and cyclical process of practical experimentation and personal reflection. The framework is adapted from the “Creativity and AI” module of Sage’s Digital Literacy course (Zaphir & Henrickson, in press). Its purpose is to be discipline agnostic; a framework which can be broadly applicable across cohorts and disciplines. Critical AI literacies require the development of students’ own ethical ideas and practical skills in using the tools; this process is designed to be adaptable in any context. Creativity has different implications and different applications in each discipline. AI can act as a useful collaborator if the user can state what and why they want to do it. Students will all benefit in the exercise of deliberately choosing which skills to offload and which to augment, and then reflecting on their choices with each use. The presentation works through one complete turn of the cycle using a worked example: the initial AI-assisted draft, the reflective prompts applied to it, the position statement the student produced, and the changed approach taken on the next attempt. Slides alternate between student artefacts and the framework stage they illustrate. Attendees will leave with the reflection prompts used at each stage and a one-page cycle template they can adapt to their own discipline and cohort.

items.abstract_text: AI is only the latest in a succession of educational technologies that have made learning easier and more frictionless, which, counterintuitively, has coincided with a population-level decline in cognitive ability and poor learning outcomes. Studies in cognitive offloading and productive struggle suggest it may be affordances of information technology exacerbated by AI that contribute to these poor outcomes. Describing the relevance of cognitive offloading, cognitive load theory and the expertise reversal effect, this paper explores the cognitive mechanisms associated with technological assistance that have been shown to affect learning, and considers pathways to redesign learning in a way that focuses on useful forms of learning friction, understood as the effortful work that consolidates learning. The paper locates these cognitive mechanisms near the learner experience where self-regulation holds the most potential to effect change when combined with educator support. The question for educators, designers and students will continue to evolve: does experiencing friction enhance learning? A heuristic is offered as a conceptual model of a process for teachers and designers to support learners at the point where cognitive offloading occurs.

items.abstract_text: The rapid integration of autonomous artificial intelligence agents, predictive trade analytics, and multimodal generative models into multinational enterprise (MNE) operations has fundamentally disrupted the foundational assumptions of International Business (IB) higher education. Traditional IB pedagogy—anchored in static comparative advantage models, retrospective case analyses, and isolated cross-cultural taxonomies—increasingly fails to prepare graduates for an era defined by algorithmic global value chains and geopolitical fragmentation. Moving beyond superficial classroom tool adoption, this study investigates how Artificial Intelligence can systematically restructure International Business education through the theoretical lenses of Institutional Entrepreneurship, Distributed Cognition, and Experiential Learning Theory. We argue that modern global business education must cultivate Symbiotic Cross-Border Intelligence—the integrated capacity to deploy, audit, and ethically govern intelligent systems across divergent sovereign, cultural, and regulatory jurisdictions. To operationalize this paradigm, the paper constructs an Adaptive Curriculum Co-Evolution Model paired with a Four-Tiered Experiential Learning Ecosystem that replaces passive lecturing with live cross-border algorithmic sandboxes, regulatory friction wargames, and multilingual stakeholder simulations. Drawing upon multi-semester pedagogical implementations across international finance, global supply chain resilience, and emerging-market entry courses, we demonstrate substantial improvements in students’ causal systems reasoning, hallucination forensics, and cross-cultural communicative agility. Finally, the paper addresses structural risks—including algorithmic monoculture, epistemic dependency, and extraterritorial data governance violations—and formulates an institutional compliance charter for business schools navigating the intelligent transformation of global commerce.
